newsitem.title: JAPAN: Change in Japan trade pattern to continue - ministry.
newsitem.headline: Change in Japan trade pattern to continue - ministry.

text.p: Structural changes in Japan's trade patterns that led to lower exports and higher imports will continue despite the yen's retreat from record highs of two years ago, the Trade Ministry said in a report on Tuesday.
The report said the relocation of factories overseas by Japanese manufacturers to combat the high yen and efforts by East Asian nations to improve their industrial bases had been key changes.
As a result, Japanese firms now exported from other countries and were procuring more goods locally, making it more difficult structurally for exports to increase and imports to decrease, it said.
In 1996, the yen weakened from 105 to the dollar at the beginning of the year to 115 yen at the end -- a significant depreciation from its jump to 79.75 yen in April 1995.

A weaker yen normally spurs exports and dampens imports as it makes Japanese goods cheaper to customers overseas and goods from abroad more expensive. It was trading at around 113.90 to the dollar at midday on Tuesday having hit a low of 127.47 on May 1.

The report said that while some manufacturers of electronic goods were considering increasing procurements from Japan because of the weaker yen, only a small minority were thinking of changing their long-term investment plans overseas.
Japan has often been attacked over its trade surplus as being the result of an over-reliance on exports for growth while it keeps its own markets closed to many imports.
Grumbling from the United States in particular has grown in recent months and U.S. officials have repeatedly warned Japan not to embark on a fresh export drive.

The report comes one day after the release of data showing that Japan's trade surplus for April rose 163.7 percent from the same month last year. Economists have said, however, that while the surplus is on a rising trend, the pace of the increase should slow later in the year.
